lead: An ocean passage is won before the start: season, boat, crew. Then it is routine, kept up daily until you clear in.

sections.title: The right ocean in the right months

qa.q: When is the best time to sail from the Canaries to the Caribbean?
qa.a: Late November to January. Plan each ocean outside its **storm season**, with the prevailing wind behind you, and go south to the steady trades before turning west.

refs: Ocean passage planning — route and season

blocks.p: Plan each ocean outside its storm season, with the prevailing wind behind you; insurance may fix the dates. Go south to the steady trades before you turn west: the shortest line is seldom the fastest. 2 850 M in the trades at 6.3 kn take 19 days, 2 650 M of light airs at 4.8 kn take 23.

sections.title: What three weeks at sea ask of her

qa.q: How much drinking water should we carry for an ocean crossing?
qa.a: Allow 3 litres a person a day for drinking and cooking, more in the tropics, plus a **50 % reserve**, split between tanks and cans. Never count on the watermaker.

refs: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

fig.note: Fix in harbour what you cannot fix at sea

list: Rig: a cracked fitting in old wire condemns it all; re-rig, carry spare wire.
Steering: a windvane uses no power; try the emergency tiller in harbour.
Chafe: move the wear point daily. Engine spares: fuel filters, impellers, belts.

blocks.p: Budget energy in amp-hours, amps × hours per load, against what solar and a towed generator give; the engine makes up the deficit. Range under power: usable litres ÷ litres an hour × speed, with a reserve for the landfall.

fig.title: Water for 5 crew, 18 days
lines: Tanks 350 L: 55 L more in cans

blocks.p: Allow 3 L of water a person a day for drinking and cooking, more in the tropics, plus half as much again, split between tanks and cans. Provision for the expected days plus 50 %; cabbage, onions, potatoes and unwashed eggs keep for weeks, stowed dry and airy and checked daily.

sections.title: Rested people make good decisions

qa.q: How do I set up a two-watch system so nobody always gets the worst hours?
qa.a: Use an odd number of watches a day, as in the **Swedish system** of five, so the watch hours rotate. Standing orders then tell the watch when to call the skipper.

refs: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

blocks.p: A shakedown of two or three days with night watches shows seasickness, skill and who follows the rules, while you can still change crew. A medical condition is planned for, not barred. Rotate the watch hours: with two watches that needs an odd number of watches a day, as in the Swedish system, five a day.

fig.title: Standing orders
lines: Call me: any ship with CPA under 2 M
Call me: wind over 20 kn, glass −3 hPa in 3 h
Clip on at night; nobody forward alone

blocks.p: **Standing orders** spare the watch from judging alone; a handover passes on course, sails, traffic and weather trend. The skipper answers for boat and crew: a schedule never outranks a forecast, a deputy lets you sleep, and you go to people in distress when you can safely. Yachtmaster Ocean covers yachts up to 24 m.

sections.title: The daily routine far from land

qa.q: What should a float plan for an ocean passage include?
qa.a: A trigger: the **float plan** you leave ashore says who calls which MRCC after what silence. Report daily in UT; if your link dies, relay through another boat before the trigger falls.

fig.title: Daily report, 1800 UT
lines: Course 265°, speed 6 kn, wind ENE 18 kn
Shore: no report for 48 h → call the MRCC

blocks.p: Leave a **float plan** ashore with a trigger: who calls which MRCC after what silence. Report in UT (zone +4: 1800 UT is 1400 aboard); if your link dies, relay through another boat before the trigger falls.

Log the position hourly; work the noon position and day's run (25 hours when the clocks go back). Back-ups: a handheld GPS stowed against lightning, sextant, an almanac for every month of the passage, tables for your latitudes, plotting sheets, a large-scale chart of the landfall. Check the compass daily by the Sun's amplitude or azimuth.

sections.title: Your own boat is the rescue service

qa.q: Should we take to the liferaft if the boat is taking on water?
qa.a: Not while she floats: stay with the boat, fight the leak, tell the MRCC early and take to the **liferaft** only when she sinks.

blocks.p: Help may be days away: clip on before you leave the hatch, with a second person awake, and give each lifejacket an **AIS MOB beacon**, seen on your own plotter. Overboard: MOB button, danbuoy, a pointer, sails down, back under power; a halyard and a winch lift the casualty.

head: Equipment
For an ocean
rows: registered to the boat, battery in date
add PLB, sat phone, water, hand watermaker
prescription drugs and a guide, with a doctor

fig.title: Abandon ship
lines: 4 Step in dry, grab bag with you

blocks.p: Stay with the boat while she floats: fight the leak, tell the MRCC early, take to the raft only when she sinks. For illness the MRCC connects you to a doctor: have position, vital signs, history and kit list ready. Seasickness tablets work only taken before sailing; a seasick crew comes off watch, clipped on, sipping fluids.

qa.q: Should I heave to, stream a drogue or use a sea anchor in a gale?
qa.a: With sea room, **heave to** when the crew is exhausted; running too fast, stream a drogue astern; with a reef to leeward, lie to a parachute sea anchor from the bow, which nearly stops the drift.

fig.note: Hove to: nearly stopped, bow off the seas
Drogue astern: stern to the seas
Sea anchor from the bow: head to sea

blocks.p: Before a gale: storm sails tried in harbour, everything lashed below, food cooked ahead, crew rested. With sea room, heave to when the crew is exhausted; running too fast, stream a **drogue** astern; with a reef to leeward, lie to a **parachute sea anchor** from the bow, which nearly stops the drift. A lee shore at night is the danger: stay out and close it by day.

sections.title: Arrive by day, with the Q flag up

qa.q: What do I do when I arrive in a foreign country after an ocean passage?
qa.a: Go straight to a port of entry under the **Q flag**; only the skipper lands, with passports, crew list, ship's papers and the last port's outward clearance. Once cleared, the courtesy flag goes up.

blocks.p: Make the landfall in daylight: slow down or heave to rather than close an unlit reef at night. A light rises at 2.08 × (√height + √eye height) miles. Old charts can be a mile out and remote lights fail: keep a wide berth. Unsure of your position, **aim off** up-current of the harbour: then you know which way to turn.

tiles.name: Atolls at night
tiles.note: wide berth, radar; gap by day

fig.note: Yellow: flown until customs and immigration have cleared you

blocks.p: Go straight to a port of entry under the **Q flag**; only the skipper lands, with passports, crew list, ship's papers and the outward clearance from the last port. Send any advance notice in local time, declare all food, and sign off crew who leave. Once cleared, the Q flag comes down and the courtesy flag goes up at the starboard spreader.
